title: Knowledge Check 4: Lessons 16-20
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 16-20 of the hermes-consultant-intermediate series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: What are the three parts of a threat model?
options: The project budget, the delivery schedule, and the written acceptance criteria
The assets, the actors who threaten them, and the trust boundaries
The model, the provider, and the terminal backend in use
The scope, the identified risks, and the rollback plan
questions.explanation: A threat model names what you are protecting, who threatens it, and the lines an actor must cross to reach it. Without that structure every security decision is a guess on the client's behalf.

questions.question: Why does agent security rely on defense in depth rather than one strong control?
options: Because a firewall placed at the network edge stops every realistic agent threat
Because the model's own safety training is sufficient to contain the agent
Because separate profiles sandbox the agent and fully contain its filesystem access
Because no single layer covers every boundary, so one catches what another misses
questions.explanation: Each layer covers a different boundary, so a gap in one is caught by another. A setup with one strong control and five gaps is a gate with an open field around it.

questions.question: How should secrets be handled in a delivery?
options: Stored in environment variables or credential files, scoped to the task, kept out of prompts
Embedded directly in the scripts so that they are always available when the agent runs at night
Written into the operating doc so that the operator knows each value by heart
Shared across every agent in the estate to make rotation simpler for the team
questions.explanation: A credential belongs in an environment variable or credential file, scoped to the narrowest task that needs it. A leaking secret is the highest-severity, lowest-effort failure, so it is the first thing a reviewer checks.

questions.question: Which responsibility belongs to compliance rather than to IT or legal during an agent rollout?
options: Provisioning the environment and approving when production changes are allowed
Maintaining the standards the organization has committed to, such as audit
Bounding the organization's liability through the contracts that it signs
Writing the marketing plan that sells the agent to the client's staff
questions.explanation: Compliance owns the rules the organization has committed to and is satisfiable by evidence, not enthusiasm. IT controls the environment and legal controls the contractual frame.

questions.question: Which sequencing practice best reflects how the IT, compliance, and legal gates should be handled?
options: Finish building the agent first, then ask each team how long its review will take
Treat the three teams as one obstacle and clear them together at the very end
Start the slow gates in parallel with the build so the channel is open at go-live
Present one technical demonstration to all three teams in a single meeting
questions.explanation: The slowest gate is the schedule, so the sticky gates are started early and run beside the build. Planning backward from go-live keeps the channel open when the agent is ready.

questions.question: When translating the same technical decision to the legal team, what should the consultant present?
options: A liability-bounded scope stating what the agent will not do
A feature demonstration that shows how capable the agent is
An audit trail and retention record that shows what the data does
A deployment plan describing where it runs and how it authenticates
questions.explanation: Legal limits the organization's exposure, so it needs the scope written as a bound on liability. A deployment plan serves IT and audit evidence serves compliance.

questions.question: Under a fixed-fee contract, who carries the estimation risk, and when is the mechanism the right choice?
options: The client carries it, because the price is fixed and known in advance
You carry it, and it fits work whose scope you genuinely know
Neither party carries it, because the price is agreed before work begins
You carry it, and it fits exploratory work you cannot yet scope
questions.explanation: Fixed-fee loads the overrun risk onto the consultant, which is fair only when the work is understood well enough to price. Exploratory work belongs under a rate instead.

questions.question: Under time-and-materials, what does the consultant owe the client in return for the client carrying the estimation risk?
options: A hard ceiling with no further billing regardless of the total effort
A guarantee that the final total will match the original estimate
Honest hours, surfaced changes, and a budget range with a checkpoint
A fixed price for each deliverable once the client scopes it out
questions.explanation: Because the client absorbs the overrun, the consultant owes transparency and a guardrail. Without a range and a checkpoint, an open-ended rate becomes a blank check.

questions.question: How should the price of a recurring agent operation be determined?
options: From the real per-run cost of the pinned model and provider, plus margin
From the market rate other vendors charge for similar agent work
From the buyer's stated budget spread across the length of the engagement
From the number of sessions the agent happened to run during the pilot
questions.explanation: The price is a claim about your unit economy, so it is built from the actual cost of the pinned configuration with margin. Numbers read from the run record beat a market guess.

questions.question: Why should acceptance criteria be written as tests rather than as descriptions?
options: They make the document look more rigorous to the client's legal team
They let both sides know what done means and can be run and counted
They let the seller state the price before the client agrees to any scope
They remove the need for an out-of-scope list in the contract
questions.explanation: A description such as accurate enforces nothing, while a test with a pass bar can be run and counted. Testable criteria turn done from an argument into a fact.

questions.question: Why is a specific scope boundary, paired with an out-of-scope list, central to protecting both sides?
options: It lets the client make additions without ever going through any process
It hides the parts of the engagement the seller remains unsure about
It gives a reference that classifies any request as in or out
It guarantees the project will finish ahead of the agreed schedule
questions.explanation: A boundary specific enough to classify any request is what lets a change be priced instead of argued. Naming what is excluded prevents the client from assuming it is included.

questions.question: What goes wrong when the payment schedule does not match the risk allocation priced into the engagement?
options: It becomes a second, conflicting agreement that overrides the risk allocation
It has no effect, because the pricing decision already governs the engagement
It automatically converts the engagement from fixed-fee to time-and-materials
It makes the statement of work unenforceable for both parties at once
questions.explanation: The payment terms are where the risk allocation becomes money changing hands. When they disagree with the pricing, the mismatch acts as a second contract that wins the argument.

questions.question: What distinguishes scope creep from normal, healthy addition to a project?
options: Creep is any addition the consultant personally finds tedious or unwelcome
Creep is addition outside the change process, so its cost is never visible
Creep is addition that makes the project run longer than a single calendar year
Creep is addition requested by a manager rather than by the sponsor
questions.explanation: Addition is normal; the problem is unmanaged addition whose cost never lands where the client can see it. The delta is only measurable against a written baseline.

questions.question: Which four steps make up the change-order discipline for a request past the baseline?
options: Quote the work, negotiate the fee, absorb the difference, and reconcile at the end
Warn the client, log the request, delay the work, and revisit it monthly
Name the delta, name the trade, get a yes, and write it into the baseline
Decline the request, escalate to the sponsor, rebaseline, and restaff the work
questions.explanation: Every request is stated as a precise delta and paired with a visible trade in time, price, or scope. The client owns the trade and the change is recorded so the baseline stays the source of truth.

questions.question: When a client disputes whether the delivered system produced a specific result, what is the effective move?
options: Run the case and let the recorded output settle it
Restate the original specification from the statement of work
Escalate immediately to the sponsor to resolve the disagreement
Appeal to the consultant's expertise and prior experience
questions.explanation: Words are claims, and a disputing client does not trust claims. Producing the artifact or running the case lets the delivered system arbitrate against its own recorded behavior.
